- **Global wind belts and ocean currents (trade winds, westerlies, volta do mar, monsoon)** [`wind_systems_ocean_currents`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/wind_systems_ocean_currents.md) — K1, use partial, make medium, accept medium. Etesian winds and the March–October sailing season are known. Greek pilots from Egypt cross to India with the monsoon since Eudoxus of Cyzicus (c. 118 BC); few ships go. Elsewhere: Ptolemaic Egypt, Red Sea ports Berenice and Myos Hormos; South Arabian and Indian sailors on the monsoon.

Lodestone attracting iron is described by Lucretius (book VI). That a floating needle points north is unknown anywhere. Pilots use sun, stars, winds and landmarks and winter in port. Local: lodestone (magnes lapis), traded as a curiosity; iron needles.

Coast-pilot books (periploi) give distances in days' sail and stadia. No log, no sandglass, no compass; a water-clock is useless on a moving deck.

Greek astronomers fix latitude on land by gnomon shadow and longest day (Pytheas at Massalia, Hipparchus' zones). It is never done aboard ship. Local: Sosigenes. Elsewhere: Alexandria and Rhodes, dioptra and armillary instruments.

- **Sounding lead, rutters and coastal pilotage** [`sounding_lead_pilotage`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/sounding_lead_pilotage.md) — K4, use correct, make easy, accept high. A lead with a tallow-filled cup is standard gear; periploi list harbours, capes and distances. Local: pilots at Puteoli and Ostia.
- **Tides and tide tables** [`tides_tide_tables`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/tides_tide_tables.md) — K2, use partial, make easy, accept medium. Posidonius at Gades tied the tides to the moon's daily course and phases. Caesar lost ships to a spring tide in Britain in 55 BC. The Mediterranean barely has tides. Elsewhere: Gades (Cádiz), Atlantic tides observed.

Caesar saw and described the Pharos in 48 BC. Ostia is an open river mouth with a sandbar; big grain ships unload at Puteoli. Caesar will plan an Ostia harbour. - **Diving bell and underwater work** [`diving_bell`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/diving_bell.md) — K2, use partial, make medium, accept medium. Breath-hold divers (urinatores) salvage cargo and cut cables. The air-filled cauldron lowered to divers is in the Aristotelian Problemata.
- **Canals and pound locks** [`canal_locks`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/canal_locks.md) — K1, use partial, make medium, accept medium. Canals without locks exist: Marius' cut at the Rhône mouth (102 BC), drainage tunnels. Caesar will plan a Tiber–Tarracina canal and an Isthmus cut (45–44 BC). Pound locks exist nowhere. Elsewhere: Han China, Lingqu canal with navigation weirs.
- **Engineered roads (Roman roads to macadam)** [`paved_roads_macadam`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/paved_roads_macadam.md) — K4, use correct, make easy, accept high. Via Appia to Brundisium, Flaminia, Aurelia, Aemilia, Domitia through Gaul. Built by magistrates and the army. A city law (Heraclea tablet, date disputed) bans most daytime wagon traffic in Rome.
- **Spoked wheels, pivoting axles and sprung carriages** [`spoked_wheel_suspension_carriage`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/spoked_wheel_suspension_carriage.md) — K3, use partial, make medium, accept medium. Spoked wheels with iron tyres; the best carriages are Gallic types (raeda, essedum). No springs or strap suspension. Throat-and-girth harness limits horses, so oxen and mules haul.
- **Saddle, stirrups and horseshoes** [`stirrup_saddle`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/stirrup_saddle.md) — K1, use partial, make easy, accept high. Cavalry ride a four-horned Celtic saddle without stirrups; hooves are unshod. Saddlers and smiths could make stirrups in days. The army is the buyer. Local: Caesar's Gallic and German auxiliary cavalry. Elsewhere: India, toe-loop stirrups.
- **Bridges (arch, truss, suspension)** [`arch_bridge_truss`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/arch_bridge_truss.md) — K4, use partial, make easy, accept high. Stone arches cross the Tiber: Pons Aemilius (142 BC), Mulvius (109 BC), Fabricius (62 BC). The army builds timber trestle bridges. No truss design, no suspension bridges. Local: Pons Fabricius to the Tiber island; Pons Sublicius, the old timber bridge.
